Family Health

Ajwain while breastfeeding: milk-supply claims and safety

Updated: October 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Ajwain, also called carom or ajowan, is used in food and traditional remedies. A small amount seasoning a meal is different from drinking concentrated preparations or taking an extract. There is no established evidence that ajwain reliably increases breast milk, enriches it or is safe at a medicinal dose for a breastfeeding parent and baby. Low milk supply deserves skilled feeding assessment rather than a herbal promise.

What ajwain is

The accepted botanical name is Trachyspermum ammi, a member of the Apiaceae family. It is a branching annual with finely divided leaves and small white or pink-tinged flowers in umbrella-like clusters. The tiny ridged dry fruits are commonly called seeds and used as an aromatic spice. Common names can be confusing: ajwain is not interchangeable with cumin, fennel or ordinary caraway.

Its aroma is associated with compounds including thymol, but composition varies between plants and preparations. The photograph shows a culinary spice, not a medicine or a guide to identifying wild plants. Growers’ descriptions of height, soil or appearance do not establish safety during breastfeeding; use clearly labelled food rather than foraging from a picture.

Food, nutrients and concentrated products

Ajwain fruits contain plant nutrients and aromatic constituents, but a pinch of spice is a small serving. Claims that it supplies abundant vitamins, minerals, protein, fibre or antioxidants should not be treated as evidence that a usual serving meets nutritional needs. An old study analysing several traditional supplementary foods, including an ajwain recipe, measured food composition and digestibility; it did not prove that ajwain itself increases milk production.

A varied diet supports the breastfeeding parent’s health. Ajwain is not a replacement for meals, treatment of a nutrient deficiency or recommended parent and infant supplements. Seeds in food, strong tea, distilled herbal water, capsules, extracts and essential oil can deliver different amounts of constituents. A recipe or a product described as natural does not provide a proven medicinal dose.

Traditional benefits are not established treatments

Ajwain has been promoted for indigestion, gas, reflux or ulcers, diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, intestinal worms and other infections; coughs, colds, throat or sinus symptoms and asthma; and urinary symptoms, kidney or bladder stones and increased urination. Other claims involve blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol and heart protection, pain, muscle spasm, back or joint symptoms, gout, headaches, seizures, relaxation, dental problems and liver health. These claims do not establish effective treatment in breastfeeding people.

Further claims include energy, sexual function, sperm quality or male fertility, withdrawal from dependence, menstrual timing or pain, heavy bleeding and supposed uterine cleansing. Laboratory antioxidant, antimicrobial or anti-inflammatory effects do not prove that swallowing ajwain treats these conditions. Plant-oil assays and rat ulcer or isolated-thymol diabetes experiments are not clinical trials of a breastfeeding parent and infant. Do not replace prescribed care or delay assessment of infection, asthma, seizures, bleeding or other illness.

Does it increase breast milk?

Ajwain is sometimes called a galactagogue, a substance intended to increase milk. Reliable evidence of a clinically useful ajwain effect, a suitable dose and infant safety is lacking. Long traditional use, a nutritious recipe or a laboratory result cannot show that a baby receives more milk. It should not be advertised as improving milk quality or guaranteeing a supply increase.

Milk production depends on several factors, including effective and regular milk removal. A clinician or lactation specialist can assess an observed feed, attachment, swallowing, feeding frequency, weight and age-appropriate nappies, alongside parent and baby health. Hormone or medicine treatment, if appropriate, needs individual evaluation; do not borrow a prescription or assume another galactagogue is suitable.

Culinary use is different from herbal treatment

An occasional ordinary food exposure is not, by itself, a reason to stop breastfeeding or discard milk. This does not establish the safety of repeated large quantities, concentrated tea, distillates, supplements or essential oil. There is no verified ajwain medicinal breastfeeding dose or universal waiting period after taking it. Ask a pharmacist or clinician before using a remedy, especially with a newborn, premature or unwell baby.

Give the product name, full ingredient list, preparation, amount and timing, and mention all medicines and supplements. Mixed products and extraction methods vary; labels, purity and contaminants can create additional uncertainty. Do not give ajwain remedies or essential oil directly to an infant, add them to expressed milk, or apply them where a baby could lick them. Keep concentrated products out of children’s reach.

Side-effect lists need careful interpretation

It is not established that ajwain inevitably causes jaundice, thyroid or liver damage, ulcers, mouth inflammation, headaches or dizziness in a breastfeeding parent or baby. Nor is there a reliable rule that using it for more than seven days dries up milk. A symptom occurring after a product may be important without proving that ajwain caused it; product mixtures, dose, contamination, medicines and other illness need consideration.

Stop a nonessential herbal product and seek advice if new rash, mouth irritation, persistent vomiting, abdominal pain or unusual drowsiness develops; seek emergency care for severe features described below. Do not test a suspected allergy by taking it again. Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, persistent symptoms or a marked supply change need medical assessment rather than treatment with another herb. Do not stop prescribed medicines without advice.

What to do about suspected low supply

Ask a midwife, paediatric clinician or qualified lactation professional to observe a whole feed and review growth, milk transfer and nappies. A baby seeming unsettled, breasts feeling softer or a small pump yield alone does not diagnose low supply. Feeding problems, illness, some medicines, previous breast surgery and other parent or infant factors may need targeted care.

Use a practical feeding and expression plan agreed with the team. If supplemental milk is needed, make sure the baby receives enough nutrition; do not abruptly remove prescribed top-ups to try an herb. Any changes should include a plan to protect milk production and check the baby’s weight and hydration. Appropriate treatment can help many families, but no food or medicine guarantees a particular result.

When the baby needs urgent help

Seek prompt same-day assessment for feeding that is worsening, fewer wet nappies than expected for age, poor weight gain, repeated vomiting, or suspected new or worsening jaundice. Jaundice needs assessment, not ajwain water or sunlight treatment. A baby with jaundice needs immediate emergency care if any one of these applies: under 24 hours old; sleepier than usual or difficult to wake; not feeding; floppy, stiff, jerking or twitching; temperature 38°C or higher or 36°C or lower, or feeling hot or cold or shivering; no wet nappies; or breathing difficulty or very fast breathing. Do not wait for all these signs.

Any baby with breathing difficulty or very fast breathing, blue or grey lips or tongue, a seizure, loss of consciousness or who is not responding normally needs emergency help now. Do not wait to see whether stopping a herb is enough. Follow emergency-service instructions and do not drive yourself when emergency transport is needed. Keep the product packaging available so the team knows what exposure occurred.

After a concerning exposure

If an infant swallows essential oil or another potentially harmful concentrated product, contact emergency services or a poison service immediately; do not wait for symptoms. If you are unsure whether an exposure is harmful, get urgent poison or medical advice. Keep the container and do not induce vomiting. A small amount of spice in a normal meal is a different situation and should not be treated automatically as poisoning.

The breastfeeding parent needs immediate emergency care for breathing difficulty, swelling of the lips or tongue, fainting or loss of consciousness, or a seizure. Severe abdominal pain, vomiting blood or black tar-like stools also need emergency assessment. Persistent vomiting, jaundice or other new concerning symptoms warrant prompt medical advice. Ask for individual guidance about feeding after a significant exposure rather than using a guessed pause or milk-discard schedule.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

If supply worries you, request an observed feed and a written nutrition and growth plan. Do not delay needed supplemental milk while waiting for a herb to work.

Before taking a medicinal ajwain product, show the clinician or pharmacist its ingredients, preparation and dose, and discuss the baby’s age and health. Do not assume another product or a traditional recipe has the same safety.

Seek prompt help for poor feeding or jaundice and immediate emergency help for the severe warning signs. Keep packaging after an exposure; do not give herbal remedies or essential oil to the baby.

How BeMama can help

Ajwain can be a food flavouring without being a proven lactation treatment. Uncertain medicinal safety does not mean every culinary exposure causes harm, and an unproven seven-day milk-loss claim should not replace a proper feeding assessment.

When to seek help

Do not give ajwain remedies or essential oil directly to an infant or replace needed feeding or prescribed treatment. Poor feeding, fewer wet nappies, poor growth or jaundice need prompt assessment. A baby with jaundice needs immediate emergency care if any one of these applies: under 24 hours old; sleepier than usual or difficult to wake; not feeding; floppy, stiff, jerking or twitching; temperature 38°C or higher or 36°C or lower, or feeling hot or cold or shivering; no wet nappies; or breathing difficulty or very fast breathing. Do not wait for all these signs. Any baby with breathing difficulty or very fast breathing, blue or grey lips or tongue, a seizure, loss of consciousness or who is not responding normally needs emergency help now. Potentially harmful concentrated-product ingestion needs immediate poison or emergency advice; do not induce vomiting.

Evidence notes updated: October 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Ajwain’s milk-boosting benefit and medicinal breastfeeding dose are not established.
  • A culinary pinch and a concentrated remedy are different exposures.
  • Traditional, laboratory and animal findings do not prove parent or infant benefit.
  • Low supply needs feeding, growth and health assessment, with adequate infant nutrition.
  • Poor feeding, jaundice or severe symptoms should not wait for a herbal remedy.

Frequently asked questions

What is ajwain?

Ajwain or carom is Trachyspermum ammi. Its small aromatic dry fruits are called seeds and used as a spice. It is not interchangeable with cumin, fennel or ordinary caraway, and a photograph should not be used to identify plants for eating.

Does ajwain increase or enrich breast milk?

A reliable clinical benefit has not been established. Traditional use and nutritional analysis of a recipe do not prove increased milk transfer to a baby. Get feeding and growth assessed rather than relying on a milk-boosting claim.

Is a little ajwain in a meal the same as ajwain tea or oil?

No. Ordinary food seasoning and concentrated or repeated medicinal use are different. An occasional food exposure alone is not a reason to stop breastfeeding, but it does not establish the safety of tea, distillate, capsules, extracts or essential oil.

Is there a safe medicinal breastfeeding dose?

No verified ajwain dose or universal waiting period has been established for breastfeeding. Discuss the exact product and exposure with a clinician or pharmacist, especially for a newborn, premature or unwell baby. Do not give remedies or essential oil directly to the infant.

Does ajwain dry up milk after seven days?

That fixed timeline is not supported by reliable evidence. A supply change should prompt assessment of milk removal, feeding, medicines and parent and baby health, not an automatic diagnosis of herbal toxicity.

Can it treat stomach problems, infections or other illnesses?

Traditional claims cover many conditions, but laboratory or animal findings do not prove clinical effectiveness during breastfeeding. Do not use ajwain instead of treatment for asthma, infection, seizures, bleeding, diabetes or another diagnosed illness.

What helps if I think my baby is not getting enough milk?

Arrange an observed feed and review of weight, milk transfer and age-appropriate nappies. Follow an individual feeding and expression plan. Keep any needed supplemental nutrition until the care team guides changes; do not remove it abruptly to try an herb.

Which signs need emergency help?

Any baby with breathing difficulty or very fast breathing, blue or grey lips or tongue, a seizure, loss of consciousness or who is not responding normally needs emergency help now. A baby with jaundice needs immediate emergency care if any one of these applies: under 24 hours old; sleepier than usual or difficult to wake; not feeding; floppy, stiff, jerking or twitching; temperature 38°C or higher or 36°C or lower, or feeling hot or cold or shivering; no wet nappies; or breathing difficulty or very fast breathing. Do not wait for all these signs. Potentially harmful oil ingestion needs immediate poison or emergency advice.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
